What he heard was the sea-gate: a dull heavy boom across the town in the rain, that he felt in his feet, and again, slow. The ram. They had got it up the water-gate stair. And the door was not giving, and he could hear it not giving. A door that is going to go makes a different noise at each blow. This made the same noise every time, like a man hammering on the side of a hill.

*Stuck.* He nearly laughed. *Leave it stuck.*

Then, from up there, a scream. It went up very high and on for longer than a man's scream should. And under it a long dry hissing whisper, like surf drawing back over shingle, which he could not name until he could. Sand, going down over the parapet a panful at a time onto the men at the ram, in at their necks and sleeves and under their mail, hot enough to make wet sacking smoke.

The ram stopped.

His teeth were together so hard that his jaw ached. He let them go.

*The lady said it was the worst thing in the book.*

Then the smell came up from the harbor: pitch, oily rag, and wet timber being made to burn. They had fired the yard. He thought of the slips and the frames in the shed loft and the house with its door on the latch and the boy asleep in it, and made himself stop, because the lane was his.

And then the third thing, which was not a sound and not a smell, but a lack of both.

Something was coming up the lane that made no noise. Men climbing a stair in the rain blow and swear and scrape. This did not. He heard feet, only feet, a great many of them on the wet stone, all together: a step, a pause, a step.

And under the feet, a voice. Thin, flat, steady, coming up out of the dark from a long way down, saying one word and then another, in Tharsian, in the level voice of a man reading figures. A bead clicked. A step. A word. A bead.

*The count.*

"Here they come," said Tuccius, quite quietly, and behind him on the steps he heard the boys' shields come up, all together, near enough.

---

The dead came round the turn of the flight below him in a row, five abreast, filling the lane from wall to wall.

He had seen the dead come up out of the harbor mud on the day of the dead, with the weed on them. These were not those. These were the other kind, clean and whole in plain grey, with Navarchy shields on their arms and short spears in their hands, their faces blank in the rain, and on every brow under the hairline, where the clerk's light caught them coming round the turn, a line of small dark letters. The rain ran over their open eyes and they did not blink. They came up one step at a time, on a count that was behind them, out of sight, with a little hooded light bobbing down there among them that stopped when they stopped.

They smelled of nothing. That was the worst of it. Wet men smell. These did not.

He let them come.

He let the first row come to within a spear's length of the step he stood on, and the second round the turn behind it, and the lane fill with grey as far down as the dark went. He did not count them. Counting was for the other side.

Then he stepped back up one step, and one more, and was in the front rank with the boys, at its middle, with his shield locked on Pullus's on one side and some other boy's on the other, and he said what he had said every morning of the winter.

"Front rank. *Push.*"

They pushed.

It was what he had drilled them for. You could not frighten the dead or hurt them enough to stop them, and if you stood and thrust at one it would come on with your point in it and kill you while you tugged. You moved them. They were heavy and stupid and walked on a count, and if you put a wall of shields into the front of them, all together, and shoved, they went back; and on a stair, back was down.

The shields went into the grey row with a sound like a cart going into a wall.

For a moment nothing moved. Tuccius felt the weight of them come onto his shield and through it into his shoulder and down his back into his bad thigh, a dead flat weight, no give in it, like leaning on a quay. The boy on his right made a noise. Pullus on his left made none at all.

"*Step,*" said Tuccius.

The second rank stepped up and put its shields to the backs of the first, and its weight with them.

"*Push.*"

And the grey row went back, not staggering, because the dead do not stagger, as a door goes back, one step down; and its heels met the shins of the row below, which had not been told to move; and for a heartbeat the two rows hung there, leaning; and then the whole top of the lane went down the flight in a heap of grey and shields and spears, slithering, with no sound but bodies and metal on stone. Not a cry. Not a grunt.

"*Step.*" They stepped down after them, one step, together. "*Push.* Spears."

The short spears went down into the heap, and the Lanciarii's long points came over the boys' heads and went down deeper, and at the house end Iason was saying something vicious under his breath and driving his point down, over and over. Nothing stopped the dead. But a dead man with a spear through the knee does not get up off a stair.

"Hold," said Tuccius. "Hold there."

They held. The heap below them stirred and heaved and began, slowly, on the count from below, to get up.

---

It went on like that for a time he never afterward could measure.

He had been in fights at sea for thirty years. A fight on a deck goes in rushes, and then everybody stands about blowing and looks for his friends. This was the same thing over and over on the same few steps in the same rain: the count coming up out of the dark, the dead getting up and coming on, some dragging a leg now, some reaching with empty hands. And the boys pushing them down.

*Push. Step. Push.*

He heard himself saying it. The words had gone so far down into him over the winter that they came up on their own, as the stroke comes up in an old rower's back when he hears a drum.

A boy in the front rank slipped on the wet and went down to one knee, and the dead in front of him reached over his shield for him, and Tuccius put his own shield-rim into the dead man's face and his lancea's butt-spike down through its foot into the crack between two steps, and pinned it there, and hauled the boy up by his collar and stood him on his feet.

"Feet wider," said Tuccius. "Under your shoulders."

"*Sir.*"

A spear came over a grey shield and went into the boy on Tuccius's right, under the arm, and the boy screamed and dropped his own spear and turned in the rank to run, and ran, up the steps past the second rank into the dark toward the Baths with his hand clamped under his arm and the blood coming between his fingers. Two more ran after him, not hurt, only running. Tuccius let them go.

"Close up," he said. "Close up. Rabirius, that gap."

The lanciarius came forward into it with his long lancea shortened in his hands, and the rank closed.

Halfway down the flight, among the dead, there was a living man.

Tuccius saw him for a moment in the rain: a Navarchy marine with a red face and his mouth open, shouting at the dead, or at the clerk behind them, or at the boys, and then the grey closed round him. The dead to wear the shields down; then the living to go through where they were worn.

His shield arm had gone dead to the shoulder. He could not feel his fingers on the grip. He looked at them, to see if they were still there, and they were.

Pullus had not moved off the wall. The dead always went for the wall, liking something at their shoulder, and Pullus had put his shield into every one of them and his weight behind it, and his big slow face under the bad helmet had not changed once. There was a cut on his cheek he did not seem to know about. He breathed through his mouth, steadily.

---

Then the count stopped.

He did not notice it at first. He noticed the dead.

The row in front of him had been coming up the last step with its spears reaching, and it did not take the next step. Not with a jolt or a stumble. All five together, as if the next figure had not been given; and there they stood, a spear's length off, with their spears half up.

Behind them, all the way down the flight to the turn, the rows had stopped too. Every one where it stood. One with a foot lifted for the next step stood on one foot.

The rain went on running down their faces.

Below the turn, out of sight, somebody was shouting in Tharsian, high, and nobody was answering.

Tuccius looked up over the roofs on the right of the lane, through the rain, to where the ridge of the biggest net-loft stood black against the sky; and there was a shape on it, kneeling, and as he looked it lifted its arms, and drew, and loosed, and knelt again.

Down below the turn, the shouting stopped.

He did not hear the arrow. He never heard any of her arrows all night. He heard only what came after: a man down there in the dark who had been reading figures, and then was not.

"She's got the clerk," somebody said behind him, in a high, cracked voice, and somebody else began to laugh, and could not stop.

"Hold," said Tuccius. "*Hold.*"

They held.

---

The living came through the standing dead like men coming through a hedge.

A score of them, perhaps more: Navarchy marines in mail and round helmets, their faces wild in the rain, shoving the standing dead aside where they could and going round where they could not. And when they came out of the front of the dead onto the last step below the boys they came all at once, roaring, which the dead had never done; and the roaring did what the dead had not done all night. It broke the boys.

Not all of them. Half the front rank. They went back up the steps in a rush, the boys, as boys will when a grown man comes at them roaring with a sword, and the rank came apart; and for a moment Tuccius was standing on the lane with a gap on his right as wide as a door, and a Navarchy marine coming through it with his sword going up.

He killed him.

He did not afterward remember how. He remembered the man's face very close, young, with rain in the cleft of his chin, and the smell of him, wet leather and garlic and fear, a living man's smell after a night of nothing; and the jar in his arms when the lancea went in. Then his foot was on the man's chest and he was pulling it out, and another was coming.

Iason was there, off the house end and across the gap, low, under the second marine's shield, with his gladius in one hand and his boot-knife in the other, fighting as they had fought in the gutters of the capital; and the marine went down the steps with Iason on top of him, and only Iason got up.

And Pullus held the wall.

The rank had gone from his right, and he stood at the wall alone with his shield up, and a marine came at him, and another; and the boy did not run, and did not fight either, in any way that Tuccius had taught him. He pushed. He put his shield into the first marine's and the weight of a boy who had hauled boats up the hard since he could walk behind it, and the marine went down the step into the man behind him, and both went down among the standing dead.

"*Push,*" said Tuccius. His voice came out of him like a bark. "*Step.* Second rank, *step.* Front rank, *close up. On Pullus. Close on Pullus.*"

And they came. The boys who had gone back up the steps came down them again, most of them, to the big lad at the wall as if he were the only fixed thing in the world, and put their shields on his, one and one and one, and the rank came shut on him like a door on its post, with Tuccius in the middle of it and his own blood in his eyes from somewhere.

"*Push.*"

They pushed. The marines went back down the step into the standing dead.

And from the ridge, through the rain, the arrows came again, one and a long breath and one; and a man in the lane with a crest on his helmet, shouting the others on, sat down on the step among the grey rows, quite slowly, and did not get up. Then another. The shout went out of the marines all at once, as wind goes out of a sail, and they were going back down the flight through the standing dead with their shields over their heads against the ridge.

The boys stood on the last step and watched them go.

Nobody followed. Tuccius did not let them. He stood with his shield arm hanging and watched the last of the living go round the turn, and leave their dead behind them, standing where the count had left them, on every step from his feet to the dark.

---

*From the book of the Navarch:*

*Third hour. They came along the yard from the beach with fire. I saw the fire before I saw the men. They put it to the third slip and to the shed of the second keel; the rain is against them; the engineer's lad and a line of the prisoners are at the shed with buckets.*

*The prisoners have not come. I record that first because it was what I watched for. Captain Varus's men called them at the steam-box wall and at the pen, in our own speech, by the Navarchy's word for a crew released, which I have not heard said aloud since I was a lieutenant. A few came, and ran along the quay toward the boats, and went. The rest stood at the wall where they eat. Some are carrying buckets for the town. He called them again. They did not answer.*

*It is Varus. I know him by his walk; he walks as he did on my deck. He has grown a beard since the Teeth. He held the lead box for me there, open, and stood at my side while it did its work, and was sick afterward over the rail, and apologised to me for it.*

*He came to the arch with perhaps thirty men. Merula and the cook held the left of it. The brothers held the right, under my window.*

*He did not attack at once. He called up to me by my title and by name, and said that the Navarchy had sent for me at its own cost, and that I was to come down. The brothers stood between him and the stair door. I did not answer. I did not know what answer the occasion required. I am writing this instead. He will think that very like me.*

*Then they came on.*

*The brothers have held the slip gate before, on the day of the dead, in the Lanciarii's line; they put their spears into the same man at the same moment, I am told, as though they had practised it. They did so again tonight. I saw it. I record that it is so.*

*Velthur fell first. A spear from the left, meant for his brother, and he stepped into it; I could not say whether he meant to, and I do not think he could have said. He went down across the foot of the stair door. Arruns stood over him. He fought over his brother's body under my window for longer than I would have thought a man could, with a spear and then with nothing, and called out in their speech the whole time, the same few words, over and over. I do not have their speech. I could not write the words down. I am sorry for it.*

*Then Arruns also.*

*Merula and the cook closed the arch over them. The arch held.*

*Captain Varus stood in the rain at the foot of the arch, out of reach of Merula's spear, and looked at the two of them for a long time. He knew where they were from. Their speech is Thessa's, and so are their faces, and we sailed from Thessa to the Teeth, he and I, with Thessa's stone in a lead box. He looked at them as if they were a figure that would not come out.*

*Then he looked up at my window. I was writing. I did not stop.*

*I believe he saw me.*

*He called his men off and went back along the yard toward the beach, at a walk.*

---

The Baths smelled of blood and broth.

Hostus had the boy on the old grey-veined slab in the warm room, with a lamp either side and the spring steaming in its channel round the walls. It was the boy who had taken the spear under the arm. His name was Cossus, Lucco's youngest, from the *Sabina*, fifteen, and very white, and biting on a folded strap with his eyes shut while Hostus sewed.

Hostus sewed as Tuccius had once seen a sailmaker sew on a sinking deck: very fast and very small and not hurrying at all. There was blood to his wrists and none on his fingers. Tuccius did not know how he managed that.

"Will he live?"

"If he keeps his hands off it," said Hostus, without looking up. "And drinks his broth. And doesn't get the rot in it, which is up to the gods and not me. The spear went in under the arm and out along the ribs. It didn't go in." He knotted, and cut. "It looks worse than it is. Most of them do. They'll all want to show it to their mothers."

"She'd have had it closed by now."

"She would." Hostus reached for a clean cloth. "She's at Stoneheart. I'm here. He'll have a scar like a rope from his armpit to his belly, and he'll be prouder of it than of anything he'll ever do in his life." He looked up then, at last, at Tuccius, with his thin stooped face very tired in the lamplight. "Sit down. You're bleeding on my floor."

Tuccius put his hand up to his face. It came away red. It was a cut over the eye, the kind that bleeds like a slaughtered pig and means nothing. He had not felt it. He sat down on the bench by the wall, and his thigh told him what it thought of the night, all at once, so that he grunted.

Along the walls on the pallets lay the others. Not many. A boy with a broken arm. A boy with two fingers gone from his shield hand, staring up at the painted fish. Rabirius the lanciarius with a sword-cut across his thigh, cursing without much interest. Two of the town with their hands in wet cloth from the pans. And on the far pallet somebody asleep under a blanket, with his mother beside him holding his hand as if it might go somewhere. Tuccius did not ask about that one.

Hostus brought him a bowl. It was the broth: mutton, with barley in it and a great deal of salt, and it was too hot.

"Drink that," said Hostus.

"I'm not hurt."

"Drink it," said Hostus, who made every man drink a bowl whether he wanted it or not; and Tuccius drank it, and it went down into him like a coal, and his hands began to shake at last, now that there was nothing for them to hold.

---

He went out into the lane at first light.

The rain had stopped. The sky over the Grey was the color of a herring's belly, and the steam was coming up off the gutters and the wet roofs, so that Cyrene stood in its own fog.

The dead were still on the steps.

He stood at the top of the lane and looked at them for a long time.

They stood where the count had left them, a row and a row, from a spear's length below his step down round the turn. The ones that had been pushed down and got up stood with their legs wrong under them and their hands half reaching. The one that had been taking a step stood on one foot. In the grey light he could read nothing of the letters on their brows, but he could see them plainly: a line of somebody's handwriting on every one.

They would stand there, he supposed, until somebody took up the count, or until they fell; he did not know which, or how long.

The boys had come out of the Baths behind him and stood in a crowd at the top of the steps, and did not go down. Pullus stood at the front with Hostus's stitches in his cheek and his helmet in his hands, looking at the face of the one he had put his shield into first and last all night.

"Who were they?" he said.

Nobody answered him. Tuccius did not know. He did not think anybody on the island knew, unless the Navarch did.

At the head of the lane, beside the step that was the fourth from the top, two of the town's women had come out of a door with a bucket and a brush, and were scrubbing the blood off the stones. They did the step as well. They did it on their knees, with their backs to the dead, and talked to each other the whole time, about bread.

---

He went down to the harbor by the crown's road, the long way round, so as not to walk past the dead.

The yard was black. The rain had saved it, the rain and Velthur's boy and a line from the steam-box wall. The third slip was scorched to the ways and stank of wet char, the shed of the second keel had lost the end of its roof, and the frames in its loft were wet through and not burned. The house stood untouched, its thatch steaming, its door on the latch.

He pushed it, and it swung. On the warm floor by the hearth, curled round himself like a dog in a coat burned at the hem, the boy was asleep. There was a little fire in the grate, built up neat. It was too neat for the boy. Somebody had come in and done it for him, and gone.

Tuccius let the door swing to on the latch and left him.

Out past the end of the yard, on the long mole, there was a ship.

She lay with her bows high on the stones of the mole and her stern in the water, canted like a drunk man leaning on a wall, her oars all anyhow along her side and her cables trailing slack. Her people stood on the mole beside her with their hands on their heads, a few score of them, and two cohort men from the mole tower stood over them with spears, looking as though they did not know what came next. There were heads in the water round her stern, sleek and dark, watching.

Proteas came up the quay steps to him out of the sea as he walked along the quay toward the slip gate. The old hunter's grey hair was flat to his skull and he moved slowly, as a man moves who has been working all night in cold water, and there was a long cut on his forearm that the sea had washed white.

"She came in for the gap at the turn of the tide," said Proteas. "Her tide." He smiled, a little. "We had been at her cables since she came to anchor. When she weighed, they would not come up. And she had come in an hour wrong, and the flood took her. She went onto the mole." He looked at the ship, with something in his face that might have been satisfaction, or only tiredness. "The others went out. Three. We fouled what we could reach. Not enough."

"Enough," said Tuccius.

"Your engineer will be pleased," said Proteas. "Another hull."

He went back into the sea without another word, down the quay steps, and was gone.

---

They had laid the brothers under the arch of the slip gate, on the stones, side by side, with their faces covered.

Merula sat on the step of the gate-tower door with his spear across his knees and his lenses folded on their cord in his hand. He was grey to the lips. There was blood dried on the haft and on his clerk's hands.

Ancus had laid one of the Lanciarii's red cloaks over the two of them and put a stone on each corner against the wind, and stood looking at it with his arms hanging, like a man who has done all the cooking there is and cannot think what comes next.

Velthur's boy sat at the brothers' feet on the wet stones with a blanket round him and their two planes across his knees, one hand on each. He had not, Tuccius thought, been asleep at all.

Tuccius stood and looked at the cloak.

Then he took off his helmet, because he did not know what else to do, and stood holding it.

"They held it," said Merula, from the step, in his dry clerk's voice. He was not speaking to Tuccius. He was speaking to nobody. "From the right. Under the window. They held it all the way." He turned the lenses over in his fingers. "I have added columns for the Survey for four years, and for the garrison before that. I know when a thing comes out." He stopped. "It did not come out. They did it anyway."

Tuccius looked up at the window over the arch.

The lamp was out. The window was grey with the morning. And at it, behind the little thick panes like the bottoms of bottles, the Navarch was standing, and looking down at the cloak on the stones, with his book in his hand.

---

He went up.

The stair was in the gate-tower, with a door at the foot that the brothers had stood in front of all night, and a door at the head that was not locked. He knocked. He did not know why.

"Come in, lieutenant," said the Navarch.

The room was small and bare and very neat: a cot with its blanket squared, a table under the window, a stool, a shelf with nothing on it but quills, cut. It smelled of lamp-oil and wet stone and ink. The Navarch stood at the window, stooped under the low beams as he must have stooped all his life under a deck, in his long black coat; and his hand, as Tuccius watched, went up to his ear for the stylus that was not there, and came down.

"You will want to know what they did," said the Navarch. "At the gate. You were not here."

"I was on the lane."

"Yes. I heard." The Navarch looked at him, courteously. "I could not see the lane. I could hear it. I wrote down what I heard. It is not as good as seeing, but it is better than nothing." He held out the book. "Here. It is all there. The gate, and the yard, and the prisoners, and the captain. You may read it."

Tuccius looked at the book. It was a plain thing, bound in grey board, a blank book that somebody had given the Navarch in the autumn, and it was a third full already, in a small upright hand with no blots.

"I read slow," he said.

The Navarch considered that.

"Then sit," he said, "and I will read it to you."

So Tuccius sat on the stool with his helmet on his knee, and the Navarch of the Southern Sea stood at his table and read him the night out of his own book, in his perfect common tongue with its Tharsian vowels, without hurrying, as a man reads a return.

He did not stop at the brothers. He did not hurry at them, either. He read them as he had read the rest.

When he had finished, he stood for a moment with the book open in his hands.

"There is one more line," he said. "I had not written it. I had been waiting until the morning, to be sure I had them right."

He sat down at the table, and dipped his pen, and wrote, speaking the words aloud as he wrote them, as he had done on his own deck, as he did everything.

"*Arruns. Velthur. Of Thessa. They held the slip gate at Cyrene for the town against the Navarchy, under my window, and died there, each covering the other.*"

He sanded it, and looked at it.

"It is not the right form," he said. "There is no form for it. I have used the form for an officer's death in action. They would not have wanted that, I think. But it is the best I have."

Tuccius looked at the book on the table between them.

"How did they know?" he said.

The Navarch looked up.

"Your people. The captain." Tuccius heard his own voice, very quiet, as it had been on the *Forward*'s deck. "They came on the one stretch of the winter we were empty. To the week. How did they know?"

The Navarch was silent. He looked at the window, and the grey morning in it, and the cloak on the stones below.

"Somebody told them," he said at last. "I do not know who. If I knew, lieutenant, I am not sure that I would tell you; I have not decided. But I do not know." He closed the book on his pen to keep the place. "I will say this. It was not anybody on this island. Nobody on this island would have had to be told what day the fleet sailed. They would only have had to look out of the window." He looked at Tuccius steadily. "Whoever it was, he was not here. He was somewhere he could not see it."

Tuccius rubbed his nose with his thumb.

He did not say *the elf.* It did not come anywhere near his mouth. He thought of the shape on the ridge in the rain, kneeling, drawing, and of the count stopping on the lane; and the thing that had come up under his ribs on the *Forward*'s deck did not come up this time, and was not going to.

"There's dead on the lane," he said. "Your people's. Standing."

"Yes. I heard them stop."

"Your clerks. In the west tower." He looked at the Navarch. "Can they walk them?"

The Navarch thought about it.

"They can count," he said. "Where would you like them walked?"

"The black beach. Below the tide-line." Tuccius stood up. His thigh told him about it. "The town'll burn them. On the Midwinter wood that's left, if there is any. It's what we do."

"Yes," said the Navarch. "I remember. I will write to my clerks; they will want it in writing." He paused. "Lieutenant. Captain Varus will write his own account of last night, and it will go to the Spire, and somebody there will total it. I would be grateful if somebody on this island also wrote one. For the other side of the page."

"I'm writing to the prince," said Tuccius. "Today."

"Good," said the Navarch, and sat down, and dipped his pen; and Tuccius went down the stair past the door the brothers had held, and round the red cloak on the stones, and knew without looking up that the Navarch was writing again.

---

He dictated the letter in the long ward at the back of the Baths in the afternoon, with the children's slates stacked at the end of the table and Cossus asleep on a pallet at the far end with his broth beside him.

Ennia wrote it, with her tongue between her teeth and the lady's good pen in her fist, in big careful letters, every one standing up straight on its own like a boy in a front rank.

He had thought about what a letter ought to have in it, and what order, all morning. Then he sat down beside her and said it as he would have said it to the prince on the quay.

*To the Prince, at Stoneheart. From Tuccius of the Lanciarii, at Cyrene.*

*Highness. Four ships of the Navarchy came out of the Grey in the night, in the rain, without lights. Halia and Proteas heard them, and the old warden Maelis saw them. We had warning. We did not ring the bell.*

*They came at the sea-gate with a ram. The seaward door had dropped in the wet and the lock was stuck, and we let it stay stuck. The town gave them Fausta's sand off the gatehouse roof. They left the ram on the stair.*

*They landed on the black beach and came up the long stepped lane for the town, with their dead in front. The boys held the lane. They pushed them down it all night. The warden shot the clerks off the ridge of the net-loft, and the dead stopped where they were, and then she shot the officers, and the rest went back to their boats.*

*They fired the yard. The rain and the prisoners put it out. The third slip is scorched and the second keel's shed wants a roof. The engineer's house is not touched.*

*The prisoners did not go with them, except a few. Most of them stayed at their pots, and some carried buckets for the town. Tell the General.*

*The merfolk fouled the cables of one ship and she came in an hour wrong on the tide and went onto the mole. We have her, and her people. Tell the engineer.*

*They came for the Navarch. They did not get him. Merula and Ancus and the brothers held the slip gate under his window. Arruns and Velthur are dead there. They died each covering the other. The Navarch saw it and wrote it in his book.*

*Of ours, a few hurt, and Hostus has them. None of the boys dead.*

He stopped there. Ennia waited with the pen up.

He thought of the other things. He thought of the question, and of putting it in. He thought of the prince reading it out at Stoneheart, in front of the men, at the foot of some mountain he had never seen, and every man in the cohort looking at every other.

He did not put it in.

*Pullus held the wall,* he said instead.

Ennia looked up at him.

"Is that all of it?" she said.

"Put *the town is kept.*"

She wrote it, and under it his name, *Tuccius*, in her straight letters, because he asked her to; and he took the pen and made his own mark below, the one he had made on every pay-roll of his life: a thing like an anchor, which a bosun had taught him on his first ship, when he was younger than Pullus and could not read.

Lucco's *Sabina* would take it west tonight, on the ebb, with two of the town's best boatmen and a sack of Fausta's bread. Six days to Stoneheart, Lucco said, if the wind held. Lucco said that about everything.

---

At dusk he went down to the black beach and stood with the town while it burned the dead.

The Navarch's clerks had walked them down in the afternoon: two pale young men in Tharsian black, blinking like owls out of the west tower, who took up the count at the top of the lane in their thin flat voices. And the rows took the next step, the first in a night and a day, and came down the long stepped lane past the town standing back against the walls, and out along the quay onto the black sand, and walked into the steaming surf below the tide-line, where the clerks stopped counting. The town built the pyre round them where they stood, of the wood stacked at the head of the beach since Midwinter, and the ram from the water-gate stair, and the stranded ship's spare oars.

Orso's mother lit it. She was the one who lit the first stack. Nobody had asked her. She came down onto the sand with a brand from her own hearth, and her jaw that the garrison had broken and Liora had mended set hard, and put it in, and stood back.

It went up slow in the wet, and then all at once.

Tuccius stood at the edge of the light with his helmet under his arm, and the boys behind him in two ranks, because they no longer knew how else to stand. Maelis stood apart at the edge of the surf with her bow unstrung and her white braid dry down her back. She did not sing.

They had had names before the letters on their brows; they had stood on some quay in Tharsis in the mornings with their mothers walking past them. Somebody kept a lamp for every one of them, in some window he would never see. He watched them burn standing, and none of them fell until the fire took their legs, and then they went down all together, as they had come up the lane.

---

He walked back along the Row in the dark.

The steam was coming up off the gutters again. At the steam-box wall the four hundred and twelve were eating Ancus's fish, quieter than usual, and some of them looked up as he went by, and one or two nodded, and he nodded back.

Up at the end of Netmakers' Row, in Prisca's upper window, her lamp was lit, looking out through the gap to the sea, for the drowned rower, as it had been every night since the squall.

And down at the foot of Rope Street, in the window over the bakehouse drying-loft, there was another.

It was a red clay garrison lamp like Prisca's, with the closed hand on its shoulder, where the sand had been. Fausta's.

He went on toward the harbor master's house. At the turn of the road he looked up at the ridge of the biggest net-loft, and the shape was there, cross-legged against the dark of the hill, with her face to the sea.

He did not lift his hand to her. He did not need to.

At the harbor master's house he stopped by the tide-board, as he did every evening, and did not touch it.

His own window was beside the door, small and square, with a shutter, looking over the head of the long quay to the gap. He had never put anything in it. He took down the lamp he had begged off Sollius at noon from the fort's stores, red clay, with the closed hand on its shoulder, and filled it, which took longer than it should, because his hands had started again; and he trimmed it, and lit it, and set it on the sill with its back to the room, looking out over the quay and the slip gate and the black water, through the gap, to the sea.

Then he sat down on the cot in the dark behind it, with his boots on, and watched it burn.

---

# Chapter Fifteen: To Be Collected

**MARCUS**

The Gullet stank of ash and wet lime, and of the sea, which went in and out of it all day like a man breathing in his sleep.

Marcus came round to it on the morning ebb in the *Forward*'s longboat, five days after the galleries, with a basket of bread for the merfolk between his feet and Nerva at the steering oar. He had not been asked. Gaius did not ask people down to his works. You came, and if you were in the way he told you so, and if you were not he gave you something to carry.

The cave mouth stood up out of the sea at the foot of the cliff, black and higher than a temple door, and the swell went into it in long green backs and came out white. The boom of it was less than it had been. He had heard it every hour of every day since the gate, through the rock of the guest hall and the floor of the clans' hall and the stone bench he slept on, a sound like a door slammed somewhere far down in a house; and now it came short, and flat, and stopped against something.

Against the *Footing*. She lay at the back of the cave where Gaius had sunk her, level, with the sea over her deck and her masts struck, and only her stern-post standing up out of the low water like a stump in a flooded field. Behind her, where the roof came down almost to the water, was the Survey's cut, and against her, in the wet black light from the cave mouth, stood the form.

It was a box of oak the size of a fisherman's house, without a top and without a bottom, braced across inside with timbers as thick as a man, and weighted down against the sunk hull with stone. The dwarves had built it in pieces in the catapult-halls, and the merfolk had sunk it where Gaius said, to within a hand.

Now it was being filled.

The work went on along a chain that started on the shingle at the cave mouth, where the lime came down from the dwarves' kilns in leather sacks and the ash from the vents in baskets, and was mixed in troughs by cohort men white to the elbow, and passed out along a staging of planks into the shallows. There the merfolk took it.

They went down with it in their arms, a sack at a time, and packed it by hand into the form, under the sea, in the dark. They came up and breathed and took another. Their hair was blue in the cave-light and their shoulders shone, and the lime was white on their forearms where it would not wash off, and they did not talk about it. Kymon was at the end of the staging with his hand flat on the water, and he touched each of them on the shoulder as they went down and again as they came up, and did not take his eyes off the place between.

Gaius was on the staging, on one knee, because the other would not bend. He had his slate and his lenses and a lump of wet mortar in the palm of his hand that he kept closing his fingers on and opening, and smelling, and once licking, like a cook with a sauce.

"Highness," he said, not looking up. "There's a sack wants carrying."

Marcus put the bread down and carried it. It was heavier than it looked, and it was wet through, and the lime burned where it touched the cut on his wrist that Liora had closed four days ago and that was a pink line now, nothing more. He carried it down the staging and handed it to a merwoman he did not know, who took it from him as if it weighed nothing and looked him in the face, and nodded, and went down. The water closed over her with hardly a sound.

He went back for another. After the third, Gaius looked up.

"You want something," said Gaius.

"I want to know when it's done."

"It's done when it's full." Gaius held up the lump of mortar. "It's set when it's set."

"How long's that?"

"Weeks." He closed his fingers on the lump, and opened them, and looked at the marks. "The halls want to know the same. Brokk asks me every night. I tell him weeks, and he goes off and tells Hulda weeks, and Hulda says *hah*, and they ask me again." He turned the lump over. "It has to cure in the wet. That's the thing about it. Every mason knows it. Your common lime mortar, you keep the rain off it. This, you put it in the sea and leave it."

"Why?"

Gaius looked at him over the lenses.

"I'll tell you," he said, "when I know."

Out at the end of the staging Kymon lifted his hand off the water and said something in the merfolk's speech, and the next of them came up, and breathed, and took the sack that was held down to him, and went.

---

The shaft was the other half of it, and the shaft was Alana's.

It went down from the head of the Long Seam to the Foot, where the great old pump-head stood in the black water with its beam and its bob and its barrel gone green: a square hole in the rock, deep enough that a stone dropped into it took a long breath before it struck. It had been the halls' sump since there were halls, and now the sea sat at the bottom of it, rising and falling twice a day, a long way down.

To get the deep iron back the halls would have to lift the sea out of the shaft once the form had shut the door behind it, and keep lifting what wept in after. One pump would not do it, nor six. Gaius wanted a stair of wheels: great treadwheels set one above another up the shaft on landings cut in the rock, each lifting to a cistern on the landing above, where the next took it up. He had drawn it in an afternoon, and done its figures in three nights. The measures were not his. The shaft had been cut and recorded by the halls' old foot, in the dwarf script, in books he could not read, and he had handed the record to Alana on the night before the galleries, and she had been reading it since.

Alana was at the oak door in the afternoon when he came, where the shaft's figures came up to be worked because a lamp could be lit there, sitting on a block of coal with the weather-book shut beside her and a slate on her knees, a stick of chalk in her fist and two dwarves crouched in front of her with their own slates, all three of them in the light of one shielded lamp. One of the dwarves was a bronze-founder from Brokk's halls, square as a stove, with no eyebrows. The other was very old and very small and had a measuring-cord coiled over her shoulder, knotted at intervals, with a bead of bronze at every knot. Neither of them was talking. Alana was.

"Then the third landing's wrong in my copy," she said, "or your cord is."

The old dwarf looked at her, and then unslung the cord and handed it to her, without a word, and Alana counted the beads under her thumb and frowned, and handed it back, and wiped out a line on her slate with the heel of her hand.

"My copy's wrong," she said. "I'm sorry. I read it by the new foot, and the book had it by the old."

"Hah," said the bronze-founder.

The old dwarf said something in their tongue, a long sentence with a great many stops in it, and the bronze-founder laughed, a short bark that went down the shaft and came back up it.

"What did she say?" said Marcus.

They all three looked round at him. He had not meant to speak. Alana pushed her hair back off her face with her chalky wrist and left a white streak along her temple.

"She said I'm the first human she's met who apologises for reading the wrong foot," said Alana. "I think it was a compliment. I'm not sure."

"It was," said the bronze-founder. "She doesn't make many."

"How far down is it?" said Marcus.

Alana looked at him. Then she looked at the old dwarf, and the old dwarf at her, and some agreement passed between them that he was not part of.

"Far enough," said Alana, "that if Gaius had built from my first copy he'd have put the bottom wheel a man's height under the water, and nobody would have known until we drowned somebody trying to tread it." She turned the slate round so he could see it, and he looked at it, and it was columns: the halls' measures in the old dwarf's hand, which was square and very black, and beside each one the same measure in Alana's, small and quick, side by side down the slate as if two clerks had been keeping one book. "It goes to Gaius tonight, fair. He says eleven wheels."

"Brokk says nine."

"Brokk will say nine at supper, because nine is a better number for the halls to hear. Gaius will say eleven, because it's eleven." She turned the slate back. "And at eleven the halls will want to know who's feeding the men who tread them." She looked at the shaft, at the black square of it going down, and at the faint shine at the bottom where the sea was. "Brokk's going to ask you that again. Before the halls."

"He's already asked me once."

"I know," said Alana. "I was there." She looked up at him, with the chalk on her temple, and for a moment she forgot the slate on her knees altogether. Then she caught herself at it, and bent her head to the old dwarf's column again.

He went away. At the turn of the gallery he looked back, and the three of them were bent over the slates again in the lamplight, with their heads nearly touching, and the old dwarf had put out one square black finger and laid it on a figure in Alana's column, and was saying something, and Alana was nodding.

He walked back up through the halls to the guest hall by the long way, past the refectory, where the children were at their porridge.

It was the king's barley still. It would be the king's barley until the last sack, and then it would not. They ate it the way they had eaten it on the first night, each bowl filled to a line cut inside it, the smallest first, sitting on long benches in rows with their feet not touching the floor, and nobody running. Their wrists had not got thicker. He stood in the door and watched them, and one of them, a girl with a plait like a rope and her face in her bowl, looked up and saw him, and put her spoon down, and looked at him gravely the whole time he stood there, without blinking, until he went.

*What will you feed my halls in the spring?*

He still did not know.

---

Fingers opened the book on the eighth night after the galleries, and by the ninth the whole mountain knew it.

It was written up in chalk on a slate the size of a door that he had begged off the catapult-halls, propped against the wall of the guest hall at the end of the coal trough, where the light was best. At the top, in his small neat capitals: *WHICH MAN FIRST SAYS YES.* Under it, the cohort, man by man, with the odds against each name; and under that, in smaller letters, the terms. A bid was a bid if it was made plain, by a woman of the halls, to a man of the cohort, in front of a witness. A yes was a yes if it was said out loud. Nods did not count. *Blushing does not count,* said the terms, at the bottom, and somebody had underlined it.

The women of Stoneheart did not say a thing sideways that could be said straight, and since the galleries, since the men had come up out of the dark with their dead on their shields, they had begun to bid.

They bid the way Brokk's founders bid on tin. A coal-cutter with arms like a smith's had walked up to Vatinius in the gate hall, in front of the scales and everyone at them, and offered him the warm end of her bed and a breakfast after, and told him what the breakfast would be. Vatinius had said that he was very much obliged to her, madam, but he was on watch. He had not been on watch. She had said, "Tomorrow, then," cheerfully, and gone off to her coal, and Vatinius had stood by the scales looking at the wall until the next sack was weighed.

Nobody had said yes. That was the joke of it, and the book. A cohort of men who had walked the stair and the Teeth and the Long Seam, and not one of them could find the word.

Marcus sat on the stone bench by the door with his back to the wall and his boots to the trough, and watched them come to the slate.

They came in twos and threes after the bathing hour, with their hair wet and their skins steaming in the cold of the hall, and stood in front of it reading, or having it read to them, and arguing. Macro's name had been struck through on the first night, with a line under it: *in another book.* So had Strabo's (*Elf*), and Rufo's, with no note at all, because there was no need of one. Florus was struck through: *too wet.* Fingers had put himself at the bottom of the slate at odds so long that the figures ran off the edge, with the note *the house does not play*. And next to the bottom, at the longest odds on the slate that were still on it, side by side: *Naevius and Lollius (together or not at all).*

"That's not fair," said Tappo, at the slate, with his cup. "They don't talk."

"That's why it's the long odds," said Fingers, from his stool.

"They'd have to say a word."

"One word each," said Fingers. "I'm a fair man."

The cousins were at the far end of the trough, side by side on the floor with their backs to the bench, as they always were, eating their supper out of one pot, each with his own spoon. Neither of them looked up at the sound of his name. Nobody in the cohort could remember hearing either of them speak.

Alana came and sat down beside him on the bench, with her hair wet from the bathing hall and plaited back tight, and her chalky slate under her arm. She looked at the board for a while.

"Who's the favourite?"

"Oppius," said Marcus. "Fingers says he's got the look of a man who's been asked before and said yes before."

"Has he?"

"He's got a baker in Cyrene who'd break his other eye," said Marcus. "So no. Fingers knows it. It keeps the bets coming."

"That's very wicked."

"It's a book," said Marcus.

She looked at the board again, and at the terms at the bottom.

"*Blushing does not count,*" she read. "Who underlined that?"

"Valeria."

Alana made a small sound in her nose and did not ask why.

The dwarf women came up from the bathing hall a little after, wet and talking, with their kilts on and not much else, and the cohort looked at a great many things that were not them. Most of them went on through toward the halls. One of them did not.

She stopped in front of the slate.

She was young for a dwarf, if Marcus was any judge, which he was not; she had no grey in her at all. She was broad through the shoulder as a door and came about to Tappo's chin, and her hair was black and hung down her back wet in two thick plaits bound at the ends with copper wire. Her forearms were covered from the wrist to the elbow in small white scars, dozens of them, like a scatter of seed, where sparks had bitten her for years and she had let them. She wore a leather apron over the kilt, and the apron was scorched.

She read the board. She read it all, top to bottom, the terms too, moving her lips slightly over the common letters, and when she had done she put her thumbs in the strings of her apron, and turned, and looked at Fingers on his stool.

"You're the bookmaker."

"Madam."

"Ketta," she said. "Of the halls. I lay the catapults on Brokk's west wall. I've watched your book two nights." She looked at the board again. "Your figures are bad."

"My figures," said Fingers, "are very good, madam. I've made a living out of them."

"Your figures," said Ketta, "are what your men think of themselves. That's a bad figure. Every bookmaker in the halls knows that." She put her hand into the pocket of her apron and brought out a bar of copper as long as her finger, stamped with a clan mark, and laid it on the stool beside him. "On the two at the bottom. Together."

The hall had gone quiet round the trough. Fingers looked at the copper for a moment. Then he looked at her.

"You understand the bet," he said. "A woman of the halls bids. In front of a witness. They both say yes."

"I can read," said Ketta.

"Then you'll know you're betting on one of the other women in this mountain finding the cousins first."

"No," said Ketta. "I'm not."

She turned round, and walked down the length of the trough, through the cohort, who got out of her way, past Tappo and his cup and Rufo with his tally-stick across his knees and Sylara beside him with her eyebrows up, to the far end, where the cousins sat on the floor with their pot between them; and she stopped in front of them, and they looked up at her. Both of them. At the same time.

"I've a big bed," said Ketta, "and it's a cold mountain. The two of you." She waited a moment. "Yes or no. I don't mind which."

The guest hall held its breath.

Naevius looked at Lollius. Lollius looked at Naevius. Something went between them, without a word, as things had gone between them for twenty years in the same pot, the same rank, the same cell.

"Yes," said Naevius.

His voice was hoarse with not being used. It was the first word anybody in the cohort could remember hearing out of him.

Lollius put his spoon down in the pot, carefully, and wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist.

"Yes," said Lollius.

The guest hall came apart.

Kaeso hit his drum, once, with the heel of his hand, by the trough, as if a stroke had landed. Tappo dropped his cup. Rufo put his head down on his tally-stick and shook, without a sound. Somebody at the back began to cheer and somebody else told him to hush, and that set them all off again, and in the middle of it Ketta stood with her thumbs in her apron and her face perfectly composed, looking at the cousins, who were looking at her, and had both of them gone a dull plum colour from the collar up, which, by the terms on the board, did not count.

Then she walked back down the trough to Fingers, and held out her hand.

Fingers paid her. He counted the coin out of his box onto the stool beside the copper bar, with the whole guest hall watching. When he had done he sat back. Marcus had seen him lose money before. He had never seen him look at someone the way he was looking at Ketta.

She scooped the coin into her apron pocket. Then she did not go.

"That's the one," she said. "Now the other."

"What other?" said Fingers.

"You," said Ketta. "That's my bid. I'll make it plain, there's a witness." She tipped her head toward Marcus on the bench, without looking at him. "Not tonight. Tonight I've the two of them, and I keep my word. After."

Fingers opened his mouth, and shut it.

"I don't know the odds," he said.

"No," said Ketta. "You don't." She looked at him a moment more, with her black plaits steaming down her back and the copper wire on the ends of them catching the coal-light. "I watched you at the bronze store," she said. "In the catapult-halls. The door that's stuck since my grandmother's time. You didn't force it. You put your ear on it and your fingers on it, and you told Brokk where it was wrong before you opened it. The cutters do that, with a seam." She shrugged, a broad slow movement of the whole shoulders. "None of your others do. Work out your odds, bookmaker. I'll wait. Not long."

She went down the trough, and held out a hand to each of the cousins, and they got up off the floor, both of them, and took one each, and the three of them went out of the guest hall into the halls together without looking back, Ketta in the middle, coming up to their shoulders, and the hall watched them all the way to the door.

At the slate Fingers sat very still on his stool with his box in his lap.

Marcus got up and went over to him. He did not say anything. He took the chalk off the ledge and held it out, and Fingers looked at it, and took it, and stood up, and drew a line through *Naevius and Lollius*, and wrote beside it, in the small neat capitals: *PAID.*

Then he looked at the bottom of the slate, where his own name was, at the odds that ran off the edge, and stood looking at it.

"Will you rub it out?" said Marcus.

"No," said Fingers. He put the chalk back on the ledge. "I'll leave it. Somebody's going to want to bet on it."

In the morning the cousins were at the trough at breakfast, side by side on the floor, eating out of one pot, each with his own spoon. Nobody asked them anything. They did not say.

---

He went up to the high grass on the tenth day after the galleries because there was nowhere left under the mountain to look for an answer.

When he came out through the low door onto the shelf the snow had come down off the peak in the night and lay across the whole of the grass, unbroken, to the walls. The vents smoked above, yellow on the white, and the wind brought the smell of them down, eggs and hot stone. The herd was in. There were only the black mouths of the byres along the foot of the cliff, with the steam coming out of them in the cold and lying along the snow, and the tracks of somebody's boots going from one to the next.

Ragna was in the third, sitting on a milking-stool in the straw with her crook across her knees and her back to the warm rock, and Macro on his heels beside her, and the two of them looking at a heifer.

The byres were warm. The warmth came up through the floor, through cracks in the back wall where the vents ran near, and the rock was wet with it, and the whole place smelled of cattle and dung and hay and hot stone and milk, so thick he could taste it. Aunt was at the far end in a stall of her own, with her one short horn, lying down with her legs folded under her like a queen.

The heifer was young, black, small even for these cattle, in a stall by herself near the door, with clean straw down. She was not lying down. She was standing with her tail out stiff and her back humped, and every little while she turned her head round to look at her own flank, as if somebody had come up behind her she did not like, and then turned it back.

"Tonight," said Ragna, without looking round. "Or tomorrow. Her first."

"I didn't know," said Marcus. "I'll go."

"Sit down," said Ragna. "You'll be in the way at the door just as much as you are in here. You came up for something."

He sat down on the straw with his back to the stall-post. Macro gave him a look that might have been a welcome, and went back to watching the heifer.

"I came up to ask what the herd can give the halls in the spring," said Marcus. "If the grain doesn't come."

Ragna was quiet for a moment.

"Your lot always ask that," she said. "Or they ask how many beasts we can kill. That's the same question, asked by a man who doesn't know it's the same question." She did not say it unkindly. "What's a herd for, princeling?"

He thought about it.

"Meat," he said. "And hides."

"Hides," said Ragna. "Yes. And milk, while there's a calf to make it. And horn, for the cups and the lantern-panes. And the dung, dried, for the fires, which you'll have seen we're short of, since the coal's under water. And the calves." She turned the crook on her knees. "Meat last. Meat's what a herd is for when you've given up on the spring. The second winter we ate the breeders. We had to. And so the third winter there were no calves, and we were hungry again, and there was nothing to eat." She looked at the heifer. "This one's the first heifer of her line since. Her mother was the only cow in her stall I didn't let them take. I stood in the door with the crook."

Macro had his hand in his beard, low down, holding on.

"So the answer," said Marcus, "is nothing."

"The answer," said Ragna, "is that if you take it out of my byres, there won't be any byres. You can have it the once." She shrugged inside her sheepskin. "Brokk knows that. He asks you anyway. He's not asking about the herd."

"No," said Marcus.

"He's asking whether you'll be here."

He had nothing to say to that, and he said it.

They sat there into the evening. A herder brought bread, and Ragna's porridge in a pot, which Macro looked at and said nothing about and then quietly took off her and put on the warm rock at the back, off the heat, and stirred, until it was something a man could eat. There was milk in it. It was the first milk Marcus had tasted since the capital, and it was hot and thick and smelled of the byre, and he drank it out of a horn cup and could not remember when anything had been so good.

The heifer lay down at dark, and got up again, and lay down.

Some time after that he slept, sitting against the post. He woke because the straw was moving under him, and the heifer was down on her side across the stall with her neck stretched out flat and her lip curled back off her teeth, and she was groaning, a long low sound like a door dragged across stone, and Macro was on his knees behind her with his sleeve rolled to the shoulder and his arm in her to the elbow, and Ragna was holding the lamp.

"One foot," said Ragna. "Only the one."

"I know."

"Where's the other?"

"I'm looking," said Macro.

The heifer heaved. Her hind leg came up and kicked out straight, hard, the way a beast in pain kicks at nothing, and caught the lamp in Ragna's hand and took it out of her fingers and across the stall, and it struck the rock and went out, and the dark came down.

The byre doors were shut against the snow. There was the warm wet stink of the place, and the heifer groaning, and the cattle down the stalls lowing, uneasy, in the dark.

"Leave it," said Macro.

"I'll get a light from—"

"Leave it," said Macro. "I don't need it. Hold her head, Highness. Sit on it, if you have to. Talk to her."

Marcus went on his knees in the straw and felt his way along the heifer's ribs to her neck, wet and hot and heaving, and her head, and the hard curve of the young horn, and put his weight across it, and talked to her. He did not know what he said. Nonsense. The kind of thing Roderic said to Thistle. Her eye was under his hand, rolling. Her breath came hot on his wrist in long groans.

Behind him in the dark Macro was talking too, but not to the heifer.

"It's not the other foot," said Macro. "It's a foot. It's the wrong one."

"What do you mean, the wrong one?" said Ragna. Her voice was very close and very level.

"There's two joints above it. The first one bends this way. The next one bends the same way." His breath went out of him in a grunt as the heifer strained. "That's not a front leg. A front leg, the knee and the fetlock go the same road. A hind leg, the hock goes the other way, like a man's heel. I know where the knife goes in." The heifer heaved again, and he stopped, and waited for it, and went on. "This one's a front leg. It's the right leg. It's just the only one that came. The other's back, along her. And the head's turned down."

"Can you get it?"

"Hold the lamp," said Macro, and then, with a sound that might have been a laugh, "Never mind."

After that, in the dark, Marcus held the heifer's head and talked nonsense to her, and listened to Macro work. He could hear it: the straw, and the man's breathing, and the wet, and the heifer groaning, and Macro talking low to himself the whole time, as if he were alone in a kitchen with a beast on the block. *Back. Back. There's the jaw. Not you. Where's your foot, then. There. That's a knee. That's your knee. Come up. Cup it. Cup it, you fool, she'll tear. There.* And once, between two heaves, very quietly, "Ragna."

"I'm here."

"Put your hand on her flank. When she pushes, tell me."

"Now," said Ragna.

"Now," said Ragna again.

And then the heifer gave a great groan under Marcus's weight that he felt go through the whole length of her, and strained, and Macro said, "*Come on*," and there was a sliding wet rush in the straw, and a smell of blood and something new, and silence.

Nothing moved.

"Is it—" said Marcus.

"Hush," said Ragna.

In the dark, in the straw, something sneezed.

The heifer lifted her head under Marcus's arms, as strong as a man, and he let go, and she swung round on her chest and lowed, a deep short questioning sound he had never heard a beast make, and was answered. A thin wet bleat. Then she was licking. He could hear it, the rough tongue going, and the little thing under it gasping and shaking its head.

"Heifer calf," said Macro. His voice was not steady. "I think. I'll know in the light."

Somebody struck a flint. It was Ragna; she had felt for the lamp, and trimmed it by feel, and lit it, and held it up; and in its light there was the young black cow on her chest in the bloody straw, licking a calf as black as she was, all legs, with its eyes shut tight against the light and its ears flat and wet; and Macro sitting back on his heels in the straw beside it, red to the shoulder, with his beard full of straw and his face wet, looking at it.

Ragna looked at him. She held the lamp up and looked at him, and her creased brown face did not change at all.

Then she put out her free hand, the one with the white burn across the back of it, and took a stalk of straw out of his beard, and dropped it.

"Heifer," she said.

Macro took hold of his beard.

Marcus went out to the byre door and opened it a little and stood in the gap with the cold on his face, because it seemed the thing to do. It was nearly morning. The snow lay blue over the whole of the high grass to the walls, and the cloud below was grey, and the vents above were dull red against the dark. Behind him in the byre he could hear the calf trying its legs, and falling down, and Ragna saying something in the dwarf tongue, softly, and Macro not saying anything at all.

He thought of the girl with the rope plait at the porridge, looking at him over her bowl.

*Meat last,* he thought. *Meat's what you eat when you've given up on the spring.*

He had not given up on it. He did not know what he had instead.

---

Macro came down off the high grass the morning after the calving, behind the milk-sledge, and by the afternoon he had the halls' kettles.

They were not his to take, and he took them. The kettle-hall was a long low cave off the gate hall, black with four hundred years of smoke, where the clans' porridge went into kettles a man could have bathed in and came out grey. The kettle-women of the halls had cooked it so through three famine winters, and saw no reason to stop. Macro went in with the milk. He stood among the kettles for some time and said nothing whatever. Then he asked for the warm rock.

There was a shelf of it at the back of the cave, where a vent ran close behind the wall: too hot to sit on, too cool to boil a pot. That evening Macro set barley on it in three of the clans' smaller kettles, with the herd's milk over it, what the sledge had brought down, and a lid on each, and went to bed. In the morning he lifted the lids. The barley had drunk the milk in the night and gone soft and pale and sweet, thick as cream, with a brown skin across the top that he folded back in with the spoon. He put in a pinch of the dwarves' salt, and nothing else, and the little ones of the halls had it first.

The kettle-women tasted what was left with their arms folded. Then they unfolded them.

The second night he set the milk out by itself along the same shelf, in the shallow pans the halls kept for curd. In the morning there was a crust of cream on every pan, wrinkled and thick and gold, and he lifted it off with the flat of his knife and laid it on the bread. He showed them the knife. He showed them the pans. He showed them the cheese going into the pot at the end, off the fire, and not at the start. An old kettle-woman with no teeth stood at his elbow and watched him do it, and said something in the dwarf tongue that made the rest of them laugh until they had to hold on to the kettles.

"What did she say?" Marcus asked Brokk, at supper.

Brokk considered it.

"That if she'd known there was a man under the mountain could do that to barley," he said, "she'd never have married."

By the third night there were women of the halls at the end of the coal trough who had not come for the porridge.

The first was the coal-cutter with arms like a smith's who had offered Vatinius the warm end of her bed. She put her empty bowl down on the edge of the trough in front of Macro, before the whole guest hall, which under the mountain is a witness.

"That's a good beard," she said. "And that was good porridge. I'll have both. My bed's warm, and there's breakfast after." She thought about it. "You'll cook it."

Macro opened his mouth to find his manners, and a kettle-woman came round the end of the trough with her ladle still in her fist.

"I bid first," she said. "This morning. At the kettles."

"At the kettles isn't in front of a witness."

"There were forty women at the kettles."

"Kettle-women," said the coal-cutter, and that settled it, for her.

At the far end of the trough a third got up on the bench to be seen: a young bellows-hand from the Forge, with soot still in the creases of her neck.

"I've a cow," she said.

The guest hall turned round to look at her.

"Half a cow," she said. "My aunt has the rest."

"He's struck through, madam," said Fingers from his stool, and pointed the chalk at the slate, where *Macro* had a line through it and *in another book* underneath. "He's in another book."

"Not in mine," said the coal-cutter.

The kettle-woman laid her ladle down on the trough. The men nearest saw her do it and got up off the bench with their bowls, unasked, and went and ate somewhere else. Then the two women came together in the middle of the floor, head to head and shoulder to shoulder, as two heifers come together at a hay rack, and shoved. Neither of them said a word. Their boots skidded on the stone.

Macro stood up with one of the small kettles in his arms.

"Mind the porridge," he said. "*Mind the porridge.*" He backed away along the trough holding it up over the cohort's heads, and the bellows-hand got down off her bench and went after him, explaining about her aunt.

Marcus did nothing at all, which took every hour of his father's court he had in him. Beside him Valeria said, out of the side of her mouth, "Do something, Highness," and he said, "I'm a guest," and she put her hand over her eyes. Alana had the weather-book open on her knee and was writing in it, fast, and not looking up. Along the bench Roderic had put down his bowl to watch, with his head a little on one side.

"I've seen less spirit at Vessa fair," said Roderic, "and lower bidding."

In the door to the halls Brokk stood with his hands hooked in his belt and his beard on his chest, shaking. He stayed where he was. "Leave them," he said, when Marcus looked at him. "It's a fair bid. Both of them are."

It was Ragna who stopped it.

She had come down with the milk-sledge that afternoon, and had been sitting at the end of the trough all the while with Macro's porridge in her bowl, eating it slowly and not looking up. Now she put the bowl down, and took her crook from where it leaned against the wall, and walked across the floor to the two women; not quickly. She stopped a pace short of them, at the edge. Then she set the crook against the coal-cutter's shoulder, and leaned on it.

The coal-cutter stepped off. She seemed not to know she had done it. The kettle-woman, with nothing left to shove, came on a pace, and Ragna turned her by the elbow with the hook, gently, until she was facing her own ladle.

"He's notched," said Ragna.

She took the kettle out of Macro's arms and walked off with it through the door into the halls, past Brokk, without looking back. After a moment Macro went after her. Where Aunt went, the herd went.

The coal-cutter looked after them, and shrugged, cheerfully.

"Tomorrow, then," she said, to the hall at large, and picked up her bowl.

"I've still got the half a cow," said the bellows-hand.

"Notched," said Valeria.

"It's a herding term, my dear," said Roderic.

"I know what it is."

---

The *Sabina* came into the cove under the mountain gate on the fourteenth day after the galleries, a little after noon, with a reef in her sail and the wind on her quarter, and her two boatmen grey with salt.

Marcus saw her from the platform before the gate, where the cohort cooked its salt pork. He knew her by her patched brown sail, which he had seen off the long quay every morning of the winter at Cyrene, and his stomach turned over before he knew why, because the mail was not due, and nobody sent a fishing boat six days west in late winter to say that all was well.

He was down the gate stair before she had her anchor down. So was half the cohort.

The older boatman handed him the packet over the side without a word. It was oilcloth, tied with a net-maker's knot and sealed with a blob of red wax with a thumb in it, and it said on the outside, in big careful letters that stood up straight on their own: *To the Prince, at Stoneheart.* There was a sack in the bottom of the boat, too, and the smell of it came up through the salt: bread, Fausta's, gone hard on the voyage.

"Is anybody dead?" said Marcus.

The boatman looked at him. He was a Cyrene man, one of Lucco's cousins. He had a face like a bollard.

"Read it, Highness," he said.

He climbed back up to the platform and walked to the edge of it, away from the fires, where the rock fell away to the cove, and broke the wax and read it there, standing, with the wind off the sea going through his cloak.

He read it twice. He did not move while he did it. The cohort had come up the gate stair behind him and stood about the platform in a crowd, and the Lanciarii with them, and the dwarves at the gate had stopped their work and were watching, and none of them came near him, and he did not look round.

*Four ships of the Navarchy came out of the Grey in the night.*

He read the names the second time. Then he folded it once, and turned round.

He did not go to the guest hall with it, or call the officers. A letter like this was not his to carry off and read in a corner and tell the men what was in it after. It was theirs. The town was theirs as much as his. More, some of them.

So he stood on the edge of the platform in the wind, with the sea behind him and the cohort in front, and read it out.

He read it as it was written, in Tuccius's words, which were plain, and in a child's letters, which were big, and he did not change anything or leave anything out. He read the four ships, and the warning, and the bell they did not ring. He read the sea-gate, and the stuck lock, and the sand. He read the long stepped lane and the boys on it, and the dead pushed down it all night, and the warden on the ridge. He read the yard, and the third slip, and the engineer's house. He read the prisoners at their pots, and *Tell the General*, and did not look at Roderic. He read the ship on the mole, and *Tell the engineer*, and did not look at Gaius either, but heard Gaius make a sound behind him that he would have known anywhere: a man told a thing he had not dared to hope.

Then he read the slip gate.

*Arruns and Velthur are dead there. They died each covering the other.*

Nobody made any sound at all.

*Of ours, a few hurt, and Hostus has them. None of the boys dead.*

*Pullus held the wall.*

*The town is kept.*

He lowered the paper.

"Who's Pullus?" said somebody at the back.

"The big lad," said Rufo. "With the boathook." He had his tally-stick in his fist, and he was looking at the ground. "Fisher's boy. Sixteen. Used to stand at the end of Tuccius's line on the quay and hold it like a sweep."

"He held the wall," said Tappo.

"Seems so," said Rufo.

Marcus held the letter out.

He did not know to whom. He held it out, at arm's length, to the platform; and Oppius came forward out of the crowd and took it. The big baker held it in his two floured hands as if it were very hot or very old, and looked at it with his one eye, at the big careful letters, and could not read one of them. Marcus knew that. Everybody on the platform knew it.

"Fausta's sand," said Oppius. "That's my Fausta."

"It is," said Marcus.

"Off her oven."

"Off her oven. In her loaf-pots. It's in the letter."

"I heard it." Oppius stood there. "I want to hear it again."

Then the men with women at Cyrene came out of the crowd, as if somebody had called them by name. Atticus, with his sling round his waist and his brown face shut. Vatinius, whose girl kept the Baths' linen, which was why he had been on watch. Two of the Lanciarii, one with a widow on the hill and one with a net-wife on the Row, who had not stayed because they had not been asked. Balbus, who had nobody, but had a room on Rope Street with a landlady who fed him. Half a dozen others, whom he had danced beside in the Haul at Midwinter. They stood round Oppius and the letter in a knot, close, with their shoulders touching, and looked at the paper none of them could read.

Pen came through them.

He came quietly, as he always did, with his ink-case under his arm. He put his hand on Oppius's shoulder.

"I'll read it to you," said Pen. "Slow. As many times as you like."

Oppius gave him the letter. The knot of men closed round Pen, and he read, in his clear quiet voice, and Marcus heard *Fausta* in it, and *the Row*, and *the hill*, and *Rope Street*, and the men saying *where?* and *what did it say about the Row?* and *read that again*; and he turned away from them and walked back along the platform toward the gate.

He was nearly there when he heard Pen behind him say, gently, to all of them, "Shall I tell them we're coming home?"

He did not stop. He went in through the gate.

---

They met in the corner of the guest hall that night, by the coal trough, where they always met when there was nothing to sit at; Marcus on the bench, and the rest of them on the bench and the floor and the edge of the trough, with the coal-glow on their faces from below.

Roderic was there, with his back to the wall and his long legs out across the floor and Valeria beside him. Gaius, with his slate and nothing on it. Liora, sitting on the floor against Gaius's knees. Rufo and Sylara. Nerva standing, because Nerva always stood. Alana, at the end of the bench, with the weather-book shut on her lap and her hand on it.

The letter was on the bench between them. It had come back to him at dusk, soft from being folded and unfolded, with a smear of flour on it from somebody's thumb.

"Tell the General," said Roderic, at last.

"I told you."

"I heard you." Roderic was looking at nothing, at the far wall of the hall, where the dwarves' marks went up the rock in rows. "They stayed at their pots. Most of them. Carried buckets." He was quiet a moment. "I spent a whole winter not knowing whether I'd done a stupid thing."

"Now you know," said Valeria.

"Now I know it was a stupid thing," said Roderic, "that came out right." He did not smile. "Somebody told them we'd gone."

Marcus looked round the circle and saw that every one of them had thought it, and that none of them was going to say anything more about it, and that Tuccius, who had left it out of his letter, had known they would think it, and had trusted them not to start looking at each other. He thought that was the best thing in the letter, after the last line. He put it away.

"The ship on the mole," said Gaius. "What class was she? Did he say?"

"He said she went on the mole."

Gaius turned his slate over in his hands. "If she went on at the top of the flood she'll be sitting up." He stopped. "The second keel's shed wants a roof. That's all. The frames'll be wet, not burned, if the rain had it. And the house." He did not finish.

"Is not touched," said Liora.

"Is not touched," said Gaius.

"Who were they," said Liora, "the two at the gate? I didn't know them. I knew the garrison men, at the Baths. I didn't know the brothers."

They all looked at Marcus. He had their names in his head now, beside the others, in the place where he kept them. He did not have to look at the paper.

"Arruns," said Marcus. "And Velthur. Of Thessa. They held the slip gate on the thirtieth day, when Liora armed them, under Valeria. And they held it again."

"Arruns and Velthur," said Liora, and nodded, once, and folded her hands in her lap. She did not say anything else.

"Maelis," said Sylara, after a while. She was leaning against Rufo with his arm across her. "From my perch."

"From your perch."

"She'll have had the clerk first. Then the officers." Sylara said it as a fact, the way she would have said the wind was in the west. "She's slow to loose. But she doesn't miss." She was quiet for a moment. "I'd like to have seen it."

At the far end of the guest hall, by the door, there was a sound of men.

Marcus looked. Oppius was in the doorway. He had not come in. He stood just inside the door with his big arms folded, and behind him in the halls outside there were others, a dozen or more, the knot from the platform and some who had joined it, Atticus and Vatinius and the two Lanciarii and the rest, in the lamplight, not talking, waiting. They had not been sent for. They had come, and stopped at the door, because the corner by the trough was the officers' and every man in the cohort knew it, and none of them would cross the floor to it uncalled.

Marcus knew what they wanted. He had known since the platform. *Shall I tell them we're coming home?*

He wanted it too.

He wanted it so badly that he could feel it in his chest like a held breath: the long quay and the steam off the gutters and Prisca's lamp in her window, the step on the lane the town walked round, Fausta's oven, the boys. He wanted to walk up the long stepped lane and see the step, and put his hand on Pullus's shoulder, and on Tuccius's, and not say anything.
